title: Physics definitions
subject: Physics
syllabus: Cambridge International AS & A Level Physics (9702)
description: Definitions and laws for AS & A Level Physics (9702), worded as the Cambridge mark schemes accept them.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a scalar quantity and by a vector quantity.
items.answer: A scalar quantity has magnitude only, whereas a vector quantity has magnitude and direction.
marks: vector quantity has magnitude and direction

items.prompt: State what is meant by a vector quantity.
items.answer: A vector quantity is a quantity with magnitude and direction.

items.prompt: State what is meant by precision.
items.answer: Precision is determined by the range in the measurements, so precise measurements have a small range.
marks: determined by the range in the measurements
alt: precise results are close together / have little scatter
items.notes: The 2016 mark scheme (s16/23 2(b)) also credited 'the size of the smallest division on the measuring instrument'.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision. (accuracy)
items.answer: Accuracy is the closeness of the measured value to the true value.
marks: closeness of the measured value to the true value
alt: the (average of the) measurements is close to the true value

items.prompt: Describe the effect of systematic errors when using a micrometer screw gauge to take readings for the diameter of a wire.
items.answer: A systematic error makes the reading larger or smaller than the true reading by a constant amount.
marks: larger or smaller than the true reading
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found. Wording from the micrometer question.

items.prompt: Describe the effect of random errors when using a micrometer screw gauge to take readings for the diameter of a wire.
items.answer: A random error causes scatter in the readings about the true reading.
marks: scatter in the readings about the true reading
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found. Wording from the micrometer question.

items.prompt: State the SI base units other than the kilogram, metre and second.
items.answer: The other SI base units are the ampere, the kelvin, the mole and the candela.
items.notes: Any two scored the mark.

items.prompt: State two properties that are possessed by both scalar and vector physical quantities.
items.answer: Both scalar and vector quantities have a magnitude and a unit.

items.prompt: Define displacement.
items.answer: Displacement is the distance in a specified direction from a point.
alt: distance from a (reference) point in a given direction
distance (from the point) in a straight line in a given direction

items.prompt: Define speed.
items.answer: Speed is distance divided by time.
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found (2015, asked together with velocity).

items.prompt: Define velocity.
items.answer: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
alt: change in displacement / time (taken)

items.prompt: Define acceleration.
items.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
alt: change in velocity / time (taken)

items.prompt: State what is meant by the mass of a body.
items.answer: Mass is the property of a body that resists changes in motion.
marks: property of a body that resists changes in motion
alt: mass is the quantity of matter in a body
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State Newton's first law of motion.
items.answer: A body continues at rest or at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.
marks: continues at rest or at constant velocity
unless acted on by a resultant force
alt: a body/mass/object continues (at rest or) at constant/uniform velocity unless acted on by a resultant force

items.prompt: State Newton's second law of motion.
items.answer: The resultant force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum.
marks: resultant force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum
alt: (resultant) force is equal to the rate of change of momentum
items.notes: Must say resultant force; allow 'equal to' for 'proportional to'.

items.prompt: State Newton's third law of motion.
items.answer: The force on body A by body B is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on body B by body A.
marks: force on body A by body B
force on body B by body A
items.notes: s21/22 2(b) and s18/23 3(d) ask how the law applies to a collision, with the same two points.

items.prompt: Define force.
items.answer: Force is the rate of change of momentum.

items.prompt: Define linear momentum.
items.answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
alt: mass x velocity

items.prompt: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
items.answer: The total momentum of a system of bodies is constant provided no resultant external force acts on the system.
marks: total momentum of a system of bodies is constant
alt: total momentum before = total momentum after for an isolated system / no (resultant) external force
items.notes: Must include the condition: isolated/closed system or no resultant external force.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an elastic collision.
items.answer: In an elastic collision there is no loss of kinetic energy.
alt: the total kinetic energy before the collision is equal to the total kinetic energy after the collision

items.prompt: State and explain the variation of the acceleration of an object as it falls through water.
items.answer: As the object falls its speed increases, so the viscous force increases and the acceleration decreases.

items.prompt: Define density.
items.answer: Density is mass per unit volume.
alt: mass / volume

items.prompt: Define pressure.
items.answer: Pressure is force per unit area normal to the force.
alt: force / area (normal to the force)

items.prompt: State what is meant by the centre of gravity of an object.
items.answer: The centre of gravity is the point where all the weight of the object is taken to act.
marks: point where all the weight of the object is taken to act
alt: the point where (all) the weight (of the body) seems to act

items.prompt: Define the moment of a force about a point.
items.answer: The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance of the line of action of the force from the point.
marks: force multiplied by the perpendicular distance
line of action of the force from the point
alt: product of the force and the perpendicular distance to/from a point/pivot

items.prompt: Define the torque of a couple.
items.answer: The torque of a couple is one of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the forces.
marks: one of the forces multiplied by
items.notes: Only asked in the 2013 papers within the range searched.

items.prompt: State the principle of moments.
items.answer: For a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.
marks: sum of the clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point

items.prompt: State the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium.
items.answer: The resultant force in any direction is zero and the resultant torque about any point is zero.
marks: resultant force in any direction is zero
resultant torque about any point is zero

items.prompt: Explain the origin of the upthrust on an object in a liquid.
items.answer: Pressure increases with depth, so the pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the pressure on the top.
marks: pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the pressure on the top

items.prompt: State what is meant by work done.
items.answer: Work done is force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force.
marks: force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force
alt: force x distance moved in the direction of the force

items.prompt: State what is meant by kinetic energy.
items.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy of a mass due to its motion.
marks: energy of a mass due to its motion
alt: energy (of a mass/body) due to motion/speed/velocity

items.prompt: State what is meant by gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: Gravitational potential energy is the energy of a mass due to its position in a gravitational field.
marks: energy of a mass due to its position in a gravitational field

items.prompt: State what is meant by elastic potential energy.
items.answer: Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a body due to its extension or compression.
marks: energy stored in a body due to its extension or compression
alt: the energy stored in a body due to extension / compression / change in shape

items.prompt: Define power.
items.answer: Power is work done per unit time.
alt: work (done) / time (taken)
energy (transferred) / time (taken)

items.prompt: Define stress.
items.answer: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area.
alt: force / (cross-sectional) area

items.prompt: Define strain.
items.answer: Strain is extension per unit original length.
alt: extension / original length

items.prompt: Define the Young modulus.
items.answer: The Young modulus is stress divided by strain.
alt: stress per unit strain

items.prompt: State Hooke's law.
items.answer: The extension is proportional to the applied force, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
marks: extension is proportional to the applied force
alt: force/load is proportional to extension/compression (provided proportionality limit is not exceeded)

items.prompt: Explain what is meant by a wire being extended elastically.
items.answer: A wire that is extended elastically returns to its original length when the load is removed.
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found (2013). Mark scheme says original length, not shape.

items.prompt: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by displacement.
items.answer: Displacement is the distance of a particle or point on the wave from its equilibrium position.
alt: distance from the equilibrium / undisturbed position

items.prompt: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by amplitude.
items.answer: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle or point on the wave.
alt: the maximum distance (of particle/point on wave) from the equilibrium position

items.prompt: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by its period.
items.answer: The period is the time for one oscillation.
alt: time for one vibration / one cycle
time between adjacent wavefronts passing the same point

items.prompt: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by the frequency.
items.answer: The frequency is the number of oscillations per unit time.
marks: number of oscillations per unit time
alt: the number of wavefronts / crests passing a fixed point per unit time
items.notes: Oscillations of the source, of a point on the wave or of a particle of the medium.

items.prompt: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by wavelength.
items.answer: The wavelength is the distance moved by the wavefront during one oscillation of the source.
marks: distance moved by the wavefront during one oscillation
alt: minimum distance between two wavefronts
distance between two adjacent wavefronts

items.prompt: By reference to the direction of propagation of energy, state what is meant by a transverse wave.
items.answer: In a transverse wave the oscillations of the particles are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of energy.
marks: perpendicular to the direction of propagation of energy
alt: vibrations/oscillations (of the particles/wave) are perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation

items.prompt: By reference to the direction of propagation of energy, state what is meant by a longitudinal wave.
items.answer: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations of the particles are parallel to the direction of propagation of energy.
marks: parallel to the direction of propagation of energy
alt: vibrations/oscillations (of the particles/wave) are parallel to the direction of energy propagation

items.prompt: State the meaning of polarisation.
items.answer: Polarisation is when the oscillations are in a single direction, perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave.
marks: oscillations are in a single direction
perpendicular to the direction of propagation
alt: oscillations are in a single plane, which contains the direction of propagation (of the wave)
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the Doppler effect.
items.answer: The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency when the source moves relative to the observer.
marks: when the source moves relative to the observer
items.notes: Must refer to the change in observed/apparent frequency.

items.term: Why light can be polarised but sound cannot
items.prompt: State why light waves can be plane polarised but sound waves cannot.
items.answer: Light waves are transverse and sound waves are longitudinal.

items.prompt: State the relationship between the intensity and the amplitude of a wave.
items.answer: The intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
marks: proportional to the square of the amplitude

items.prompt: State the principle of superposition.
items.answer: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.
marks: two or more waves meet at a point
resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements
alt: waves meet/overlap (at a point); (resultant) displacement is the sum of the individual displacements

items.prompt: State what is meant by the diffraction of a wave.
items.answer: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave into the geometrical shadow as it passes through an aperture or by an edge.
marks: spreading of a wave into the geometrical shadow
passes through an aperture or by an edge
alt: wave passes through an aperture or by an edge and spreads

items.prompt: State what is meant by interference.
items.answer: Interference is the sum of the displacements of overlapping waves.
marks: sum of the displacements of overlapping waves
alt: when two (or more) waves superpose/meet/overlap the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacement of each wave

items.prompt: State what is meant by coherent waves.
items.answer: Coherent waves have a constant phase difference between them.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a node of a stationary wave.
items.answer: A node is a position of zero amplitude.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an antinode of a stationary wave.
items.answer: An antinode is a position of maximum amplitude.

items.prompt: State the conditions required for the formation of a stationary wave.
items.answer: Two waves of the same type, travelling at the same speed in opposite directions, overlap, and the waves have the same frequency.
marks: travelling at the same speed in opposite directions

items.term: How a stationary wave forms on a string
items.prompt: Explain how a stationary wave is formed on a string.
items.answer: The wave travels along the string and reflects at the fixed end, and the incident and reflected waves superpose.

items.prompt: State two ways in which a stationary wave differs from a progressive wave.
items.answer: A stationary wave has nodes and antinodes, it does not transfer energy, and different points on it have different amplitudes, whereas all points on a progressive wave have the same amplitude.
marks: different points on it have different amplitudes
items.notes: Any two points scored.

items.prompt: Explain how the pattern of bright and dark interference fringes is formed in a double-slit experiment.
items.answer: Light diffracts at the two slits. The light from each slit superposes at the screen. Where the phase difference is zero a bright fringe is formed, and where the phase difference is 180 degrees a dark fringe is formed.
marks: phase difference is zero a bright fringe
phase difference is 180 degrees a dark fringe
items.notes: Any three points scored.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an electric current.
items.answer: Electric current is the flow of charge carriers.
alt: movement of charge carriers

items.prompt: Define the coulomb.
items.answer: The coulomb is the ampere second.

items.prompt: State what is meant by quantisation of charge.
items.answer: Charge exists only in discrete amounts, which are integral multiples of the elementary charge.
alt: charge exists in discrete and equal quantities
items.notes: The 2016 mark scheme accepted 'charge exists only in discrete amounts'.

items.prompt: Define potential difference.
items.answer: Potential difference is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge.
marks: energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge
alt: work done / charge
items.notes: Must say energy (or work done) per unit charge.

items.prompt: Define the volt.
items.answer: The volt is the joule per coulomb.

items.prompt: Define the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source.
items.answer: The e.m.f. of a source is the energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven around a complete circuit.
marks: energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy
alt: energy per unit charge

items.prompt: Define resistance.
items.answer: Resistance is potential difference per unit current.
alt: potential difference / current

items.prompt: Define the ohm.
items.answer: The ohm is the volt per ampere.

items.prompt: State Ohm's law.
items.answer: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across the conductor, provided that the temperature remains constant.
marks: current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference

items.prompt: State Kirchhoff's first law.
items.answer: The sum of the currents into a junction is equal to the sum of the currents out of the junction.
marks: sum of the currents into a junction is equal to the sum of the currents out of the junction
alt: the (algebraic) sum of the currents at a junction is zero

items.prompt: State Kirchhoff's second law.
items.answer: The sum of the e.m.f.s is equal to the sum of the potential differences around a closed loop.
marks: sum of the e.m.f.s is equal to the sum of the potential differences
alt: the (algebraic) sum of the e.m.f.s and p.d.s is zero around a loop/closed circuit

items.term: Why the p.d. is less than the e.m.f.
items.prompt: Explain, in terms of energy, why the potential difference across an external resistor is less than the e.m.f. of the cell.
items.answer: Some energy is dissipated in the internal resistance of the cell.
marks: energy is dissipated in the internal resistance

items.prompt: State what is meant by fundamental particle.
items.answer: A fundamental particle is a particle with no internal structure, which cannot be broken down into anything smaller.
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State what is meant by isotopes.
items.answer: Isotopes are nuclei having the same number of protons with different numbers of neutrons.
alt: different forms of the same element
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found (2015).

items.prompt: Explain why the neutron is classed as a baryon and a pion is classed as a meson.
items.answer: A baryon such as the neutron consists of three quarks, and a meson such as the pion consists of one quark and one antiquark.
marks: baryon such as the neutron consists of three quarks
meson such as the pion consists of one quark and one antiquark

items.prompt: State a similarity and a difference between an up quark and an up antiquark.
items.answer: They have the same mass, but their charges are opposite in sign.

items.prompt: Describe two differences between the decay of a nucleus that emits a beta-minus particle and one that emits a beta-plus particle.
items.answer: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes to a proton and an electron antineutrino is also emitted. In beta-plus decay a proton changes to a neutron and an electron neutrino is also emitted.

items.prompt: State the change in quark composition of a nucleus when it emits a beta-minus particle.
items.answer: A down quark changes to an up quark.
marks: down quark changes to an up quark

items.prompt: State an observation about beta decay that is explained by the existence of neutrinos.
items.answer: The beta particles emitted from the nucleus have a continuous range of kinetic energies.

items.prompt: Define the radian.
items.answer: The radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.
marks: arc equal in length to the radius
at the centre of a circle
alt: angle subtended where arc length is equal to radius

items.prompt: State what is meant by centripetal acceleration.
items.answer: Centripetal acceleration is acceleration perpendicular to the velocity.
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a field of force.
items.answer: A field of force is a region of space where a particle experiences a force.
marks: where a particle experiences a force

items.prompt: Define gravitational field strength.
items.answer: Gravitational field strength is force per unit mass.
items.notes: Also asked as 'Define gravitational field.' (w22/42 1(a), s23/41 1(a)(i)) with the same answer.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a line of force in a gravitational field.
items.answer: A line of force in a gravitational field shows the direction of the force on a small test mass.
marks: direction of the force on a small test mass
alt: direction of acceleration of a (small test) mass
path in which a (small test) mass will move

items.prompt: Define gravitational potential at a point.
items.answer: Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point.
marks: bringing a small test mass from infinity
alt: work done per unit mass moving mass from infinity (to the point)
items.notes: Must have work done per unit mass and the idea of moving a mass from infinity.

items.prompt: State Newton's law of gravitation.
items.answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
marks: proportional to the product of the masses
inversely proportional to the square of their separation
items.notes: Must refer to point masses.

items.prompt: State the features of the orbit of a geostationary satellite.
items.answer: A geostationary orbit is above the Equator, from west to east, with a period of 24 hours.
items.notes: Asked as 'state three features' or 'two other features'. Others accepted: one particular orbital radius, circular orbit.

items.prompt: Explain why the gravitational potential near a point mass is negative.
items.answer: The gravitational potential is zero at infinity. The force between masses is attractive, so work is done on a mass to move it away to infinity.
marks: work is done on a mass to move it away

items.term: Why g is constant near the surface
items.prompt: Explain why, for changes in height near the Earth's surface, the gravitational field strength may be considered to be constant.
items.answer: Changes in height are much less than the radius of the Earth, so the radial field lines are almost parallel.
marks: much less than the radius of the Earth

items.prompt: Explain why, at the surface of a planet, the gravitational field strength is numerically equal to the acceleration of free fall.
items.answer: Acceleration is force per unit mass and field strength is force per unit mass, so they are equal.
marks: Acceleration is force per unit mass and field strength is force per unit mass

items.term: How a satellite stays in orbit
items.prompt: Explain how a satellite may be in a circular orbit around a planet.
items.answer: The gravitational force of attraction between the satellite and the planet provides the centripetal force on the satellite.

items.prompt: State what is meant by two objects being in thermal equilibrium.
items.answer: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium when there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them.
marks: no net transfer of thermal energy
alt: the bodies are at the same temperature

items.prompt: Define specific heat capacity.
items.answer: Specific heat capacity is the thermal energy required per unit mass per unit change in temperature.
marks: thermal energy required per unit mass
alt: thermal energy per unit mass to cause a temperature change
thermal energy per unit change in temperature

items.prompt: State what is meant by specific latent heat.
items.answer: Specific latent heat is the thermal energy per unit mass required to change the state of a substance at constant temperature.
marks: change the state of a substance at constant temperature

items.prompt: Define specific latent heat of fusion.
items.answer: Specific latent heat of fusion is the thermal energy per unit mass required to change a substance between solid and liquid at constant temperature.
marks: change a substance between solid and liquid at constant temperature
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: Define specific latent heat of vaporisation.
items.answer: Specific latent heat of vaporisation is the thermal energy per unit mass required to change a substance between liquid and gas at constant temperature.
marks: change a substance between liquid and gas at constant temperature
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: Explain why temperature measured using a liquid-in-glass thermometer is not a measurement of thermodynamic temperature.
items.answer: The measurement depends on the properties of the liquid used.
marks: depends on the properties of the liquid

items.prompt: State what is meant by an ideal gas.
items.answer: An ideal gas is a gas that obeys pV proportional to T for all values of p, V and T, where T is the thermodynamic temperature.
alt: a gas that obeys pV = constant x T
gas obeys pV/T = constant
items.notes: Must say thermodynamic (kelvin) temperature.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the Avogadro constant.
items.answer: The Avogadro constant is the number of particles per unit amount of substance.
marks: number of particles per unit amount of substance
alt: the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12

items.prompt: State what is meant by a mole.
items.answer: A mole is the amount of substance that contains the same number of particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.
marks: same number of particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.
items.answer: The molecules are in continuous random motion, the volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas, there are no forces between molecules except during collisions, all collisions are perfectly elastic, and the time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions.
marks: volume of the molecules is negligible
no forces between molecules except during collisions
time of a collision is negligible
items.notes: Asked for two (s23/41) or three (w24/42), 1 mark each.

items.prompt: Explain how molecular movement causes the pressure exerted by a gas.
items.answer: Molecules collide with the walls of the container. The momentum of a molecule changes during the collision, so the wall exerts a force on the molecule and the molecule exerts a force on the wall. Many molecules exerting forces across the area of the wall cause the pressure.
marks: collide with the walls of the container
wall exerts a force on the molecule
molecule exerts a force on the wall
Many molecules exerting forces across the area of the wall
items.notes: Any three points, 1 mark each.

items.prompt: Describe the motion of molecules in a gas, according to the kinetic theory of gases.
items.answer: The molecules move randomly, at constant velocity in straight lines between collisions.
marks: constant velocity in straight lines between collisions

items.prompt: State what is meant by the internal energy of a system.
items.answer: The internal energy of a system is the sum of the potential energy and kinetic energy of its molecules, which are in random motion.
marks: sum of the potential energy and kinetic energy of its molecules
items.notes: Must have both potential and kinetic energy and refer to random motion.

items.prompt: State the first law of thermodynamics.
items.answer: The increase in internal energy of a system is equal to the work done on the system plus the energy transferred to the system by heating.
marks: energy transferred to the system by heating
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found. Symbols to identify: U increase in internal energy, q heating, W work done on system.

items.term: Internal energy of an ideal gas
items.prompt: Explain why the internal energy of an ideal gas is equal to the total kinetic energy of its molecules.
items.answer: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the molecules. In an ideal gas there are no forces between the molecules, so their potential energy is zero.
marks: sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the molecules

items.prompt: Explain why, for an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is directly proportional to the change in thermodynamic temperature.
items.answer: In an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so there is no potential energy. The internal energy is therefore only the kinetic energy of the molecules, and the mean kinetic energy is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.
marks: no intermolecular forces, so there is no potential energy
only the kinetic energy of the molecules
mean kinetic energy is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature

items.prompt: State what is meant by simple harmonic motion.
items.answer: Simple harmonic motion is motion in which the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement and is in the opposite direction to the displacement.
marks: acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement
alt: acceleration is always directed towards a fixed point

items.prompt: State, by reference to simple harmonic motion, what is meant by angular frequency.
items.answer: Angular frequency is 2 pi multiplied by the frequency, or 2 pi divided by the period.
alt: 2 pi f
2 pi / T

items.prompt: Explain what is meant by the natural frequency of vibration of a system.
items.answer: The natural frequency is the frequency at which a body vibrates when there is no resultant external resistive force or driving force acting on it.
marks: frequency at which a body vibrates
no resultant external resistive force or driving force
alt: frequency at which an object vibrates when free to do so

items.prompt: State what is meant by damping.
items.answer: Damping is the loss of total energy of an oscillating system due to resistive forces.
items.notes: The 2019 mark scheme accepted 'loss of energy'.

items.prompt: State what is meant by resonance.
items.answer: Resonance is when an object oscillates at maximum amplitude when the driving frequency equals its natural frequency.
marks: driving frequency equals its natural frequency

items.prompt: State what is meant by an electric field.
items.answer: An electric field is a region of space where a charge experiences an electric force.
marks: region of space where a charge experiences an electric force
alt: region where a (stationary) charge experiences an (electric) force

items.prompt: Define electric field strength.
items.answer: Electric field strength is the force per unit positive charge.
items.notes: Also asked as 'Define electric field.' (s23/41 1(a)(ii), s24/41 5(a)) with the same answer.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a field line (line of force) in an electric field.
items.answer: A field line in an electric field is the path or direction in which a free positive charge will move.
marks: path or direction in which a free positive charge will move
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: Define electric potential at a point.
items.answer: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in moving a positive charge from infinity to the point.
marks: moving a positive charge from infinity
alt: work done per unit charge moving positive charge from infinity (to the point)
items.notes: Must say positive charge and from infinity.

items.prompt: State Coulomb's law.
items.answer: The electric force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
marks: directly proportional to the product of the charges
inversely proportional to the square of their separation
items.notes: Must refer to point charges.

items.prompt: State one similarity and one difference between the gravitational potential due to a point mass and the electric potential due to a point charge.
items.answer: Both are inversely proportional to the distance from the point and both are zero at infinity, but gravitational potential is always negative whereas electric potential can be positive or negative.
marks: electric potential can be positive or negative

items.prompt: State the relationship between electric potential and electric field strength at a point.
items.answer: Electric field strength is equal to the negative of the potential gradient.

items.prompt: State a similarity between the gravitational field lines around a point mass and the electric field lines around a point charge.
items.answer: Both have radial field lines.

items.prompt: Define the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor.
items.answer: Capacitance is the charge on one plate per unit potential difference between the plates.
alt: charge / potential difference
items.notes: Worth 3 marks in s18/41 7(a): charge / potential difference, charge on one plate, p.d. between the plates. Often 2 marks, with the last two points together.

items.term: Why a capacitor stores energy, not charge
items.prompt: Explain why a capacitor is said to store energy but not charge.
items.answer: The plates carry equal and opposite charges, so there is no resultant charge. The positive and negative charges are separated, so energy is stored.
marks: positive and negative charges are separated

items.prompt: State uses of capacitors in electrical circuits.
items.answer: Capacitors are used to store electrical energy, for smoothing (reducing the ripple on direct voltages), to block d.c., in timing circuits, for tuning and in oscillator circuits.
items.notes: Asked for any two uses (s19/41 6(a), 2 marks) or any three (w20/41 6(a)(ii), 3 marks).

items.prompt: State what is meant by a magnetic field.
items.answer: A magnetic field is a region of space where a force is exerted on a moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnetic pole.
marks: region of space where a force is exerted
moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnetic pole

items.prompt: Define magnetic flux density.
items.answer: Magnetic flux density is the force per unit current per unit length on a wire carrying current perpendicular to the magnetic field.
marks: current perpendicular to the magnetic field
items.notes: Three points: force per unit length, force per unit current, current perpendicular to the field. Any two scores 1 mark.

items.prompt: Define the tesla.
items.answer: The tesla is one newton per ampere per metre, where the current is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
marks: current is perpendicular to the magnetic field

items.prompt: Define magnetic flux.
items.answer: Magnetic flux is the product of the magnetic flux density and the area, where the area is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
marks: product of the magnetic flux density and the area
area is perpendicular to the magnetic field
alt: flux density x area x sin(angle) where the angle is between the field direction and the plane of the area

items.prompt: Define magnetic flux linkage.
items.answer: Magnetic flux linkage is the product of the magnetic flux density, the area perpendicular to the field and the number of turns.
marks: product of the magnetic flux density

items.prompt: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
items.answer: The induced e.m.f. is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.
marks: induced e.m.f. is directly proportional to the rate
of change of magnetic flux linkage
alt: induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of cutting of magnetic flux
items.notes: Must say rate of change of flux linkage.

items.prompt: State Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction.
items.answer: The direction of the induced e.m.f. is such as to oppose the change that caused it.
marks: oppose the change that caused it

items.term: Why a charge moves in a circle in a magnetic field
items.prompt: Explain why the path of an electron in a uniform magnetic field is the arc of a circle.
items.answer: The magnetic force is always normal to the velocity and its magnitude is constant, because the speed is constant, so it provides the centripetal force.

items.prompt: Explain how a uniform magnetic field and a uniform electric field may be used as a velocity selector for charged particles.
items.answer: The electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other. The particles enter the fields with velocity normal to both fields, and particles with the selected velocity pass through with no deviation.
marks: at right angles to each other
selected velocity pass through with no deviation

items.prompt: Explain why a Hall probe is made from silicon rather than copper.
items.answer: Silicon has a much smaller number density of charge carriers, so the Hall voltage is greater.
marks: smaller number density of charge carriers

items.prompt: By reference to heating effect, explain what is meant by the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current.
items.answer: The r.m.s. value of an alternating current is the steady direct current that produces the same heating effect as the alternating current.
alt: for an alternating voltage: the constant voltage that dissipates the same power as the mean power of the alternating voltage (w21/41 9(a))
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found for the current wording.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the frequency of an alternating current.
items.answer: The frequency of an alternating current is the number of cycles per unit time.
marks: number of cycles per unit time
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State what is meant by rectification.
items.answer: Rectification is the conversion from a.c. to d.c.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a photon.
items.answer: A photon is a packet or quantum of energy of electromagnetic radiation.
alt: discrete amount of energy of electromagnetic radiation

items.prompt: State what is meant by the photoelectric effect.
items.answer: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a surface when electromagnetic radiation is incident on it.
alt: electromagnetic radiation/photons incident on a surface cause emission of electrons

items.prompt: State what is meant by work function energy.
items.answer: Work function energy is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.
marks: energy required to remove an electron
alt: energy to remove an electron with zero kinetic energy

items.prompt: State what is meant by the threshold frequency.
items.answer: The threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that causes emission of electrons from a surface.
marks: emission of electrons from a surface
items.notes: Must say electromagnetic radiation or photon, not just light.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the de Broglie wavelength.
items.answer: The de Broglie wavelength is the wavelength associated with a moving particle.
marks: wavelength associated with a moving particle
alt: a particle has a wavelength associated with it that depends on its momentum

items.prompt: State three pieces of evidence provided by the photoelectric effect for a particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation.
items.answer: The maximum energy of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency but does not depend on the intensity, the rate of emission depends on the intensity, there is a frequency below which no electrons are emitted, and emission is instantaneous.
marks: does not depend on the intensity
rate of emission depends on the intensity
frequency below which no electrons are emitted
items.notes: Any three points, 1 mark each.

items.prompt: Explain how the photon model of electromagnetic radiation accounts for the threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect.
items.answer: Photons are discrete packets of energy, and the energy of a photon depends on the frequency. An electron can only absorb a single photon, so emission is only possible if the photon energy is at least the work function.
marks: energy of a photon depends on the frequency
photon energy is at least the work function

items.prompt: Explain why most of the emitted photoelectrons have a speed lower than the maximum.
items.answer: Energy is required to bring an electron to the surface of the metal.
marks: Energy is required to bring an electron to the surface

items.prompt: Explain how an emission line spectrum provides evidence for the existence of discrete energy levels in an atom.
items.answer: Each photon energy has a corresponding frequency. A change in electron energy level emits a single photon, whose energy equals the difference in energy levels. Discrete frequencies must come from discrete energy changes, which imply discrete energy levels.
marks: photon energy has a corresponding frequency
energy equals the difference in energy levels
discrete energy changes, which imply discrete energy levels
items.notes: Any three points, 1 mark each.

items.prompt: State what electron diffraction shows about the nature of electrons.
items.answer: Moving electrons behave like waves.

items.prompt: Define mass defect.
items.answer: Mass defect is the difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its nucleons when they are infinitely separated.
marks: difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its nucleons

items.prompt: State what is meant by the binding energy of a nucleus.
items.answer: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy required to separate the nucleons of the nucleus to infinity.
marks: energy required to separate the nucleons
alt: energy released when nucleons come together from infinity to form a nucleus

items.prompt: State what is meant by radioactive decay.
items.answer: Radioactive decay is the spontaneous emission of particles or radiation from an unstable nucleus.
marks: spontaneous emission of particles or radiation

items.prompt: Explain what is meant by the decay being random.
items.answer: Random decay means it cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay.
marks: cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay
alt: there is a constant probability of decay of a nucleus

items.prompt: Explain what is meant by the decay being spontaneous.
items.answer: Spontaneous decay means the decay of a nucleus is not affected by external environmental factors.
marks: not affected by external environmental factors

items.prompt: Define radioactive decay constant.
items.answer: The decay constant is the probability of decay of a nucleus per unit time.
marks: probability of decay of a nucleus
alt: the fraction of the (number of undecayed) nuclei that will decay per unit time

items.prompt: Define half-life.
items.answer: Half-life is the time for the activity of a sample to halve.
marks: time for the activity of a sample to halve
alt: time for the number of atoms/nuclei to be reduced to one half

items.prompt: State what is meant by nuclear fusion.
items.answer: Nuclear fusion is when two small nuclei join together to form one larger nucleus.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a nuclear fission reaction.
items.answer: Nuclear fission is when a single large nucleus divides to form smaller nuclei.
marks: single large nucleus divides to form smaller nuclei
items.notes: Extra marking points seen: initiated by neutron bombardment; binding energy per nucleon increases.

items.prompt: Define specific acoustic impedance.
items.answer: Specific acoustic impedance of a medium is the product of the density of the medium and the speed of ultrasound in the medium.
marks: product of the density of the medium and the speed
items.notes: Must give both density and speed in the medium.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the attenuation of an ultrasound wave.
items.answer: Attenuation is the reduction in power or intensity of the wave as it passes through the medium.
marks: as it passes through the medium
alt: loss of intensity/amplitude/power (of the wave)

items.prompt: Explain what is meant by a tracer.
items.answer: A tracer is a substance containing radioactive nuclei that is introduced into the body and absorbed by the tissue being studied.

items.prompt: Explain what is meant by annihilation.
items.answer: Annihilation is a particle interacting with its antiparticle so that mass is converted into energy.
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State, for an X-ray image, what is meant by sharpness.
items.answer: Sharpness is the ease with which edges can be distinguished.
marks: ease with which edges can be distinguished
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the contrast of an X-ray image.
items.answer: Contrast is the difference in degrees of blackening between structures.

items.prompt: Explain the main principles behind the use of ultrasound to obtain diagnostic information about internal body structures.
items.answer: Pulses of ultrasound are reflected at boundaries between media. The reflected pulses are detected by the ultrasound transducer and are processed and displayed. The time delay gives information about the depth of the boundary and the intensity of the reflected pulse gives information about the nature of the boundary.
marks: time delay gives information about the depth
intensity of the reflected pulse gives information about the nature of the boundary

items.prompt: Explain the principles of the generation of ultrasound waves for use in medical diagnosis.
items.answer: A piezo-electric (quartz) crystal is used. An alternating p.d. across the crystal causes it to vibrate, and resonance occurs when the frequency of the p.d. matches the natural frequency of the crystal, which is in the ultrasound range.
marks: alternating p.d. across the crystal causes it to vibrate
resonance occurs when the frequency of the p.d. matches the natural frequency

items.prompt: Explain the principles of the detection of ultrasound waves used in medical diagnosis.
items.answer: A piezo-electric crystal is used. The ultrasound makes the crystal vibrate, which produces an alternating e.m.f. across the crystal.

items.prompt: Explain why ultrasound used in medical diagnosis is emitted in pulses.
items.answer: The same transducer emits and detects the ultrasound and cannot do both at the same time, so detection occurs in the time between emitted pulses, which lets the reflected signal be distinguished from the emitted signal.
marks: cannot do both at the same time
detection occurs in the time between emitted pulses
reflected signal be distinguished from the emitted signal
items.notes: Any two points scored.

items.prompt: Explain how X-rays are produced for use in medical diagnosis.
items.answer: Electrons are accelerated by an applied p.d. and hit a metal target. X-rays are produced when the electrons decelerate.
marks: X-rays are produced when the electrons decelerate

items.prompt: Explain why a continuous spectrum of energies of X-ray photons is produced.
items.answer: Electrons decelerate on hitting the target, producing X-ray photons. There is a range of decelerations, and the photon energy depends on the size of the deceleration.
marks: photon energy depends on the size of the deceleration

items.prompt: State how, in an X-ray tube, the intensity of the X-ray beam and its hardness are controlled.
items.answer: The intensity is controlled by varying the filament current, and the hardness is controlled by varying the accelerating potential difference.
marks: intensity is controlled by varying the filament current
hardness is controlled by varying the accelerating potential difference

items.prompt: Outline the principles of CT scanning.
items.answer: X-rays are used to scan the body in sections, from many angles. The image of each section is two-dimensional, and images of many sections are combined to give a three-dimensional image.
marks: image of each section is two-dimensional
images of many sections are combined

items.prompt: State what is meant by the luminosity of a star.
items.answer: The luminosity of a star is the total power of radiation emitted by the star.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a standard candle.
items.answer: A standard candle is an astronomical object of known luminosity.

items.prompt: State what is meant by redshift.
items.answer: Redshift is the apparent wavelength of light from a star being greater than the known value, due to the movement of the star away from the observer.
marks: movement of the star away from the observer
items.notes: Only one mark scheme found.

items.prompt: State Hubble's law.
items.answer: The speed of recession of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from the observer.
marks: is directly proportional to its distance
speed of recession of a galaxy
items.notes: Identify the symbols: speed is the recession speed of the galaxy and distance is the distance of the galaxy from the observer.

items.prompt: State Wien's displacement law.
items.answer: The wavelength of maximum intensity is inversely proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.
marks: wavelength of maximum intensity is inversely proportional to the thermodynamic temperature

items.prompt: Explain how redshift leads to the idea that the Universe is expanding.
items.answer: Redshift is the increase in observed wavelength. Radiation from distant galaxies is observed to be redshifted, which shows that the galaxies are moving apart, so the Universe must be expanding.
marks: distant galaxies is observed to be redshifted
items.notes: Any three points, 1 mark each.

items.term: Hubble's law and the Big Bang
items.prompt: Explain how Hubble's law and the idea of the expanding Universe lead to the Big Bang theory of the origin of the Universe.
items.answer: All parts of the Universe are moving away from each other, and more distant objects are moving away faster, so matter must have been close together and very dense in the past.
marks: more distant objects are moving away faster
